title: Rethinking Environments for Long-Horizon Work — Rayan Garg, Theta Software
talk_summary: Theta Software discusses how to define and measure long-horizon agent tasks, focusing on environment complexity, ambiguity, and judge-based verification. The most transferable content is their approach to LLM judges as agents with read-only environment access, queryable trajectories, and rubric QA.

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of stuffing the trajectory into a single LLM call, they give the judge agent the same harness/tools as the worker (read-only) so it can inspect actual environment state (CI logs, deploy logs, DB) to verify correctness.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the judge has access to the environment in the same way uh with some important safeguards... we don't want the judge to make an accidental mutation

takeaways.what_they_do: Long trajectories are stored in a database and enriched with metadata/phases (log-reading phase, coding phase, verification phase) so the judge can query critical steps and failure points rather than reading raw context.
For every rubric they run basic tests (gold solution passes, no-op fails, variance across runs) plus coverage and expert-agreement checks before trusting the judge.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Gold, no op variance. These are tests you want to be considering regardless for your verifiers

takeaways.what_they_do: Judges inspect the trajectory, not just final state, to catch reward hacking like reading hidden tests or escaping sandboxes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: agent can escape a sandbox maybe see privilege information it shouldn't be seeing about maybe a hidden test suite

takeaways.what_they_do: Dynamic rubrics give partial credit by assuming an earlier wrong step was correct and grading downstream work independently.
takeaways.evidence_quote: grading a test assuming like if you got the first part wrong, let's just assume it's correct, did they get the rest of the part right?

takeaways.what_they_do: They argue long-horizon is scalar and warn that chaining unrelated independent tasks inflates horizon without measuring real capability; sequential state-dependent tasks are the hard ones.
takeaways.evidence_quote: one task can you know maybe be made by artificially long horizon by chaining together unrelated independent tasks
